hints: All copies of the target sit next to each other. Could you describe the first copy and the position just after the last copy using a 'first index whose value is ...' rule?
Use a lower-bound binary search twice: first = lowerBound(target) (first value ≥ target) and last = lowerBound(target + 1) - 1. If first is out of range or does not hold target, return [-1, -1].

1. Write lowerBound(x): binary search on [0, n) for the first index with nums[i] >= x.
  2. first = lowerBound(target).
  3. If first == n or nums[first] != target, return [-1, -1].
  4. last = lowerBound(target + 1) - 1.
  5. Return [first, last].

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: Scan the array, noting the first and last time you see the target.

approaches.name: Better
approaches.idea: Binary search for any copy, then walk left and right. Fast normally but O(n) if the whole array is the target.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: Two lower-bound binary searches: one for target, one for target + 1.

explain: With nums = [1,2,4,4,4,7,9], target = 4: lowerBound(4) is 2 (the first value ≥ 4), and nums[2] == 4, so the target exists. lowerBound(5) is 5 (the 7), so the last 4 is at index 4. Answer [2, 4]. For target 5, lowerBound(5) = 5 holds 7 ≠ 5, so we return [-1, -1]. Watch the empty array: lowerBound returns 0 == n, which is handled by the range check.
recognize: Sorted with duplicates + first/last position of a value → two boundary (lower-bound) binary searches.
